speechtext: For a copy of all orders in council passed since the outbreak of war which amend, suspend or otherwise alter the operation of any statute or statutes passed by the parliament of Canada, and a list of all statutes so effected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL AMENDING OR SUSPENDING STATUTES
speechtext:
The clerk of the, privy council informs me that amendments or suspensions of the nature asked for by my hon. friend are very few and they are resorted to only in cases of emergency. On the other hand, approximately 24,000 orders in council and 13,000 treasury board minutes have been passed since the outbreak of war. The production of papers requested in this notice of motion would involve a prohibitive amount of time and labour as it entails the consultation of each individual order in council. The motion which my hon. friend moves is very

similar to a question asked on May 19, 1941, which was acknowledged. I would suggest to my hon. friend that he have a talk with the clerk of the privy council about the matter to see if in some other way he cannot get the information he desires, but certainly to pass the order as it stands would involve an amount of labour which I do not think would be justified at this time.

maintopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL AMENDING OR SUSPENDING STATUTES
speechtext: Naturally I do not want a list of all orders in council. Possibly the hon. member for Waterloo South has given expression to a view that a large section of the public holds, and I think it is a point of view that has to be very carefully considered. The reply made to the hon. member for Gaspe last week was that he should give the information which he had to the minister of the department concerned, and if the minister thought the information to be of a kind which rendered a secret sitting advisable it would be so arranged by the government. I am advised that the information conveyed to the minister, in his opinion and the opinion of the cabinet-I can speak for the cabinet because I was present at the discussion-does not warrant the calling of a secret sitting.
As to my hon. friend's suggestion that we should have secret sessions at stated times, I think the public would be inclined to take the view that so far as sittings can be open they 
should be open, and that the government should resort to secret sittings only where there appears to be the strongest of reasons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 15, consideration in committee of a resolution to provide sums not exceeding $2,000,000,000 for the year ending March 31, 1943, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. McCann in the chair.

On May 11 the minister made certain remarks, recorded on page 2328 of Hansard, which seem to me to deserve some comment.
The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) asked the following question:
It seems to me only fair that something should be done to put those men-
Referring to the men working on farms.
-on an equal basis with their brothers and cousins who have gone to the cities and are enjoying much higher wages.
The minister replied as follows:
We did give some consideration to the question of a bonus, but it was felt that it would be almost impossible to work out any kind of bonus scheme that would be at all adequate. If you fixed a certain amount, in one part of the country it would be a pure gift; it would be much too high. On the other hand, in some areas that I have particularly mentioned, if a bonus were paid to farm labour to keep men on the land or attract them to the land, it would not be enough to counterbalance the superior attractions of high wages that would pull men from the farms into war industries.
Again the minister used the following words:	.
But there is a difference between equality of contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort and equality of sacrifice. I cannot think of any scheme that can bring about equality of sacrifice in time of war and at the same time make for maximum effectiveness.
May I interrupt this quotation just long enough to ask the minister why he has come to that conclusion. Why should maximum effectiveness be any more easily attainable when men are not making equality of sacrifice?
I utterly fail to follow the minister's line of thought there.
There is not equality of remuneration or reward either.	There is no equality of
remuneration between the soldier, sailor or airman, and the young man who works in a

War Appropriation-War Services
war industry at a high rate of pay; or between the man in the war industry and the man on the farm who has his difficult task to perform. They are all essential to the effectiveness of the war effort, but there is not equality of remuneration and there is not equality of reward. The man who enlists voluntarily has his. own remuneration and his own reward. It is inside him. He knows that he answered the call of his country when the call came. When this conflict is all over he will remember, even if everyone else has forgotten, that he answered when the call came. That is his reward, and that reward cannot go to anyone except the volunteer. So these conceptions of equality of sacrifice and equality of remuneration are easy to talk about, but the thing with which I am sure every hon. member is concerned is maximum effectiveness, even though that has to be achieved at the expense of such things as equality of sacrifice.
Again the idea in the minister's mind seems to be that in order to obtain maximum effectiveness you must depart from the principle of equality of sacrifice. I do not agree with the minister in any respect with regard to that matter. Surely it is not going to add to the effectiveness of our war effort if we are to have inequality of sacrifice, inequality of remuneration, and inequality of reward. The minister speaks as though the problem had been taken up and found difficult, and therefore had been left unsolved and neglected or laid aside. That is simply not good enough in this country at the present time. It may be impossible to bring about equality of sacrifice or equality of reward1, but certainly it is not impossible to give adequacy of reward. There are altogether too many people who have the idea that only our fighting men should be sacrificed; that without earning any great reward, they should be expected to face a future over which they have no control whatever. The idea seems to be that the next in line for sacrifice without reward is the man on the farm. Where such nonsensical ideas had their origin I cannot understand. These people, our fighters and our farmers, are of the greatest value to the country; these are the people who should be most adequately rewarded.
I feel that right now, without waiting for this session to close, we should definitely lay down the principle that every man who serves in the armed forces of this country must be guaranteed the means of establishing and maintaining a home. The pittance that these men receive at the present time certainly will not enable them to do that. Canada must have homes. How on earth can the British race survive, in competition with other races that have sense enough to realize the value of children, if the British race will not likewise realize the value of children and will not
enable their people to raise them? It is time we woke up, as a race, before we are eliminated from the competition. Canada must have homes and children. Those children must have the opportunity of growing into useful citizens. I feel that what the minister has said requires a great deal of explanation.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
speechtext:
There is not a great deal that I can add to what I stated on May 11, when I made the remarks to which the hon member for Lethbridge has referred. Our war effort is not a onesided effort. We have set our war objectives very definitely; we have indicated the various purposes of that war effort. Perhaps I might state them again. In the main they are threefold. We should raise the strongest armed forces possible, in the army, the navy and the air force, both as to number and as to quality of personnel, so that our fighting forces may be as effective as possible both in defensive and in striking power. That, I think, might be stated as our war objective as far as the armed forces are concerned. To send armed forces overseas without the necessary equipment would be the height of folly. Therefore we have another war objective. We must produce as much in the way of ships, planes, tanks, guns and other munitions of war and war supplies and equipment as it is possible for this country to produce. We have a double duty now in this regard; for not only do we have to produce munitions of war for our own armed forces, but we have entered into an obligation to supply Britain with a billion dollars' worth of munitions and supplies for her armed forces. Thirdly, we have set as a war objective the production of as much in the way of essential foodstuffs as can be transported overseas.
I have stated three war objectives, one relating to the armed forces, the army, the navy and the air force; the second relating to the production of munitions of war, and the third to the production of essential foodstuffs. Each of these objectives must be attained if this country is to make an all-out war effort, and we must move toward the attainment of these objectives concurrently.
Now, having stated the objectives and the necessity of moving forward to these objectives concurrently in the interests of the maximum effectiveness of our war effort, I am able to reply further, if any reply is necessary, to the hon. member for Lethbridge with respect to the matter of equality of sacrifice. If these

War Appropriation-War Services
objectives of our war effort are to be attained, it must be done through the use of adequate man-power for the respective purposes of these objectives. I would ask the hon. member for Lethbridge what equality of sacrifice is possible between, let us say, a young man who enters the air force as a member of a fighting crew, whose days may be numbered from the very moment he enlists, and the young man or older man who works in a munitions plant at $5, $6, $7 or $8 per day. What equality of sacrifice is possible between our airmen, our soldiers and our sailors who offer their lives, and the farmer, who while he is doing his essential work is on his farm? What equality of sacrifice is possible under these circumstances? Yet we must have men in our fighting services, and we have-I say it to the credit of Canadian youth-men volunteering their services in the fighting forces, in the army, in the navy and in the air force. The sacrifice they make is the greatest sacrifice of all; for they offer their lives; many of them have given their lives.
In order to have maximum effectiveness of the war effort we must also have the production of the necessary munitions of war. We must also have production of the necessary food supplies, not only to keep our own nation alive, but also to supply Britain and our other allies. These are essential war purposes without which this country could not make an all-out war effort. But there is no equality of sacrifice in the matter. The farmer, while he is performing his essential work in that part of our war objective, is not making a sacrifice equal to that of the airmen or the soldiers or the sailors I have mentioned, and no farmer in this country would claim that he is. He knows he is not. Nor is any person who is working in a munitions plant making a sacrifice equal to that of the airman, the soldier or the sailor. To say that men in the munitions plants are in the front line in the same way as the soldiers, sailors and airmen is nonsense.
Why the difference in wages, then?

I am dealing with
equality of sacrifice. There may be equality of contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort, and that is very necessary indeed. But there is a difference between equality of contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort and equality of sacrifice.
Some are getting paid for very little contribution.

Men do not enlist for pay; men enlist for other reasons. They enlist out of a sense of duty. They do it in the air force, they do it in the army, they do it in the navy. They are not thinking of equality of sacrifice; they are ready to make the greatest of all sacrifices. They did it in the last war, and they are doing it in this one. I am getting tired of the expression "equality of sacrifice". If it could be brought about, yes; but the very nature of war makes it impossible, because the sacrifice the one makes is in a field where he offers his life, and the one the other makes is in another field. Both are necessary for the purposes of war. One man gives of his best through his skill and labour. There may be equality of contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort, but that is a vastly different thing from equality of sacrifice.
There cannot be equality of sacrifice in war and maximum effectiveness in the war effort at the same time. Let me illustrate what I mean. Take for example two young men in a war industry, both of whom are of the same age, both physically fit, and both of the highest possible value, let us say, to the armed forces. One of them has been in the plant for years, and has become a highly skilled and trained precision tool man who could not be replaced in that plant by anyone else in less than two or three years. The other young man has been in the plant only a short time. He is not essential to war industry, nor to that purpose in the war effort that I mentioned.
It is the purpose of selective service to place persons in that field of activity in which each can make the greatest contribution to the war effort. If we are thinking of the maximum effectiveness of the war effort we will take the man who recently came into the war industry and place him in the armed forces. We might for the same reason leave the other man in war industry, because he is essential to it. Each of those men makes an equal contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort.
They should be paid the same, then.

But their equality of
sacrifice is not the same.

Should they not be paid the same, though?

War Appropriation-War Services
The question of pay is a totally different matter.
But there is discrimination.

I am dealing with the expression "equality of sacrifice", and I should like to put that phrase before the Canadian people so that they will stop talking about equality of sacrifice in war and maximum effectiveness of war effort at the same time. The two ideas are inconsistent with each other. If we could have equality of sacrifice in time of war, I would be in favour of it, but the very nature of war makes impossible equality of sacrifice among all persons who make their contribution to the success of the war effort.
Are we not all-
Do not interrupt me, please. War demands of its youngest and strongest men the greatest of sacrifice-unfortunate, indeed; but that is war.
Many of them are in the factories.

If we are to make the most effective war effort these are facts we must recognize. I want to make a distinction between equality of sacrifice in time of war and equality of contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort. We can have in a war equality of contribution to the effectiveness of the war effort, but I for one cannot see how we can have equality of sacrifice.

I have two duties to fulfil. In the first place I wish to congratulate the minister upon what he has just said and upon the way he has acted as the head of his department. He has had fine legal training and besides that he possesses a deep knowledge of parliamentary traditions. When hon. members ask for information he tries to get it if it is available. In the second place I wish to express my deep gratefulness to my colleagues for the kindness they show to the member for Temiscouata whenever he rises to speak or to ask any questions.
They are very proud of you.

This spirit of fraternity is shown by them all, including the hon. member for Wateloo South (Mr. Homuth).
I should like to ask the minister to see that a correction is made in the translation of paragraph 3 of C.P. 2252. The English text reads:
No male person wholly or mainly employed...
The French text reads:
Aucune personne de l'un ou l'autre sexe...
A correction should be made.
If it is possible to secure it, I should like to have some information about the Frenchspeaking boards which are now sitting in the various camps. This may come under the Department of National Defence, but if it happens to come under the minister's department, I would ask him to let me have the information. Until it is changed, the law regarding defence in this country is section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act. I shall not discuss this section because an amendment is to be brought before us. One thing I regret deeply is that "0 Canada" is not considererd any longer as the national anthem, but was considered in that way, although semi-officially, even when conscription was decided upon in 1940.
I hold in my hand the first edition of the national war services regulations of 1940. The present minister was not in charge of the department at that time, since he was sworn in on June 11, 1941. These regulations were submitted to council on August 27, while information regarding the farmers was reported to the minister in charge only two weeks afterwards, on September 12. A number of the higher officials of various departments contributed to that report, especially the deputy minister of agriculture, the deputy minister of fisheries, the deputy minister of mines, the deputy minister of transport and the timber controller. The report is dated September 4, but it was sent to the registrars only , on September 12.
There is a difference between the Militia Act, which is to be found on the statute book, and the 1917 conscription act and regulations and the 1940 regulations. In the first place there were exemptions, and now there are mostly postponements. I have a list of the general exemptions under the Militia Act and under the 1940 regulations. They covered the physically unfit, members of the clergy, the judiciary and the army. Exemptions were provided for members of police forces and fire brigades, for wardens and officers of prisons and lunatic asylums, members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and Mennonites, Doukhobors, and conscientious objectors. In the Militia Act, exemptions were provided for eight other classes of people, such as the members of the king's privy council, members of the executive councils of the provinces, deputy ministers of the federal and provincial governments, telegraph clerks when actually employed, officers and clerks regularly employed in the collection of the revenue, professors in colleges and universities, and teachers in religious orders, the only son of a

War Appropriation-War Services
widow being her only support, and pilots and apprentice pilots during the season of navigation.
I have the particulars of a case which is even more deserving than that of the only son of a widow. This is a boy whose father and mother have died. The details of this case are set out in a memorandum which I will send to the minister. -He has three grounds for postponement. First, he is the only support of his younger brothers and sisters; second, being a mechanical technician his services are indispensable in industry, and third, his health is bad. The other day I phoned to Quebec city to ask the national war services board to reconsider its decision in this case. The member of the board who answered me told me that he was looking after war industry only. I asked about the other member, and he told me that he was looking after farm hands and farmers only. I asked about the chairman of the board, and he told me that he was away for three weeks. I have nothing to say against the members of this board, but the point is that at the present time there is a quorum of two members only to do its work. When one member is away it is easy for the other two to reconsider any case that might be submitted to them.
I find that there were exemptions worth considering in the Borden conscription act of 1917. This act was based upon the British Military Service Act of 1916, being chapters 5 and 6, George V. This act deals with exemptions which were considered to be in the national interest. The grounds of exemption were as follows:
(a)	That	it	is	expedient	in	the	national
interest that the man should instead of being employed in military service be engaged in other work in which he is habitually engaged;
(b)	That	it	is	expedient	in	the	national
interest that the man should instead of being employed in military service be engaged in other W'ork in which he wishes to be engaged and for which he has special	qualifications;
(c)	That	it	is	expedient	in	the	national
interest that, instead of being employed in military service, he should continue to be educated or trained for any work for which he is then being educated or trained;
(d)	That serious hardship-
This is another consideration:
-would ensue, if the man were placed on active service, owing to his exceptional financial or business obligations or domestic position;
(e)	111 health or infirmity.
Then it goes on to deal with conscientious objectors. The two reasons mentioned in the clauses I have just read are surely deserving of consideration, because very serious hardship may fall upon the dependents if they have no other means of livelihood.

There is another exemption which is not precisely mentioned as such, although in practice it works out that way. Section 4 (1) of the national war services regulations provides:
Subject to the provisions of these regulations, every male British subject who is or who has been at any time subsequent to the first day of September, 1939, ordinarily resident in Canada-
-shall be liable to undergo military training; but the phrase "ordinarily resident" is not defined in section 3 of the regulations which deals with interpretations. I think it is important that the phrase should be defined so that we shall know just what length of residence in Canada is required. According to section 16 of the interpretation act;
No provision or enactment in any act shall affect, in any manner whatsoever, the rights of His Majesty, his heirs or successors, unless it is expressly stated therein that His Majesty shall be bound thereby.
That, is right. It means that the law of the land shall apply to all of us in this country except his majesty and the royal family. Therefore it is of the utmost importance to have a ruling on this point, I would thank the minister for a clear interpretation of "ordinarily resident", so that there may be no misunderstanding whatever about the phrase. In my humble view the national war services regulations should apply to every British citizen who is now resident in Canada or who comes here for the duration of the war. I can see no reason why any British citizen should not be subject to these regulations.
I think the regulations should also provide exemption in cases where there are already three or four members of the family on active service. I know an old gentleman who is a general store keeper in the country, and a farmer as well. He has one son in charge of his business and three other sons in the army, one being in England, one in Nova Scotia and the other in Newfoundland. Of course a postponement has been granted to the son who is at home, but in cases of this kind where many sons of the family are in the service, postponement should automatically be granted for the son remaining at home.
There is another reason why the Borden act was better than these regulations, and that is that it provided for an appeal from the decisions of the board, and not merely one appeal, but there was a possibility of a third appeal in case the second appeal did not render justice to the applicant. Under these regulations the decision of the board is final and conclusive. The decision of the

War Appropriation-War Services
board is always final, of course, but it is not always conclusive, and there is a reason for my saying that. Without wishing to say anything unpleasant about anyone I may point out that it is impracticable for a judge who has to sit at various places and preside for two or three weeks in the month over civil or criminal courts to hear all the cases under these regulations that come before him as the chairman of the board. It would be very easy for the department to appoint for this purpose some retired justice of the king's bench or superior court, an older gentleman who is not now on active duty on the bench, and who would have enough time to consider each case on its merits.
Of course all applications for postponement are not equally deserving. There are some that deserve particular consideration, and a judge who is absent for two or three weeks during the month from the place where the board sits finds on his return that his desk is piled so high with files that it is physically impossible for him to go through them all and get the true picture in each case. I therefore make two suggestions to the minister in that regard. The first is that he replace all the judges now on the boards by retired judges of either the superior court or the king's bench, so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, and by retired judges of similar tribunals in the other provinces. My second suggestion is that at least one court of appeal be provided where the applicant can have any wrong redressed by a superior tribunal. If the government were under the impression when these regulations were passed that they would have less trouble if no provision were made for an appeal, by now they must realize they were mistaken because they have probably had more trouble and more representations by reason of the fact that the rulings of the board are final.
I wish to impress upon the committee the fact that farmers have a case which is most deserving of consideration. I entirely agree with what the minister said about equality of sacrifice. I know personally a number of young men who would like to enlist but who cannot on account of the responsibilities they have at home. They are like the boys who have beautiful sweethearts but cannot marry because they have to look after their parents. If they leave, the padlock will be put on the farm because the aged people will find it impossible to cultivate the land.
An excellent article has been written on this matter by a journalist of note, a former president of the press gallery, who I believe is a personal friend of the minister, Mr. Emile Benoist of Le Devoir. He wrote at full length
on the matter and expounded very well the case of farmers and fishermen. This is a serious matter. It has been discussed by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) himself, and among other clippings I have one from the Montreal Gazette of February 27:
Canadian farmers asked to produce more foodstuffs; Agriculture Minister Gardiner urges maximum capacity at Breeders Banquet at Mount Royal Hotel, Montreal.
I have already had occasion to emphasize to the minister the fact that farming should not be considered a seasonal occupation. The minister will remember that my contention received support. I am sure there were representations by many other members, but to my personal knowledge my representations were supported by the Prime Minister and by the late minister of justice, and he agreed to it. Now farming is not considered as only a seasonal occupation but is described as a seasonal and essential occupation. In the province of Quebec it is essential but it is not seasonal, or rather it is seasonal in all seasons. The minister knows that in our part of the country the farmers are those who rise earliest and go to bed latest, and it is a full-time job the year round. They have a lot to do and their work is different from that of the farmers in some other parts of the country who have no cattle and work with tractors. After the harvest their year is finished. At home, however, the animals are not like camels; they have to be fed every day and it takes a long time. The farmers have all sorts of things to do, and their work keeps them busy all the time.
I have received very instructive letters on this subject and have sent copies to all ministers to inform those who were not so familiar with the farm problem regarding the work of our farmers. Of course, the statement that was made by the Prime Minister on March 24 brought some relief to the farmers and they expected that it would be easier for them to have their case settled in the future. I greatly appreciate the support I have received from the minister and the Prime Minister in connection with this problem, which is vital not only to the civilian population but also to the army and to our allies. The farmers were greatly disappointed when another statement was made by the Minister of Labour in relation to the one that had been made a couple of days before by the Prime Minister. Then the Minister of National War Services made a statement-if I am wrong I hope he will correct me-that those on the land on March 23 were to be considered prima facie farmers, and evidence to the contrary had to be brought agairrt



War Appropriation-War Services
that presumption. This is what was understood from his statement, which was widely publicized in the country. A boy was on the farm on March 23. He was prima facie a farmer, and it was up to the Department of National Defence or anyone else to show that on that day he was not a farmer and was not essential to agriculture. But the interpretation we have now in some cases is that the board decides of itself that although the man was on the farm on that very day his services are not required for agriculture. That is a very bold thing, because the importance of the man on the farm is obviously relative and when I say that I want to explain myself. You cannot always judge the importance of the farmer's work by the number of his horses, the number of his cattle, or the number of his sheep. Not only that; it is important to see whether the farmer is a bona fide farmer, and if he is he should qualify for postponement, at least, as he has no right to exemption now. He should be qualified for postponement. I have here a communique given by the minister on April 17. I have not the English text, but the French. On page 2 I find the following:
When the applicant has shown that he is a person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture within the meaning of the amended regulations, it is mandatory upon the board, subject to the exceptions hereinafter mentioned, to grant the postponement order. Furthermore, the postponement order is until further notice and it constitutes an allocation of the applicant to agriculture rather than to military service.
And it goes on. That was the change. In the first place, the onus probandi was against the farmer applicant, and now it is against the state; therefore it is up to the state not only to show but to establish that the farmer is not necessary to agriculture if his request for postponement is to be denied. This is the way it works in Montreal. I am informed that an adjournment is granted by the board, or by the registrar for the board, on the sworn statement that a farmer's son or farm hand was working on the farm on March 23. In my view such procedure is in accord with the statement made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of National War Services when they interpreted the regulations or the law. Therefore the regulation should be amended. Too much discretion is given to the board. Subsection 3 of section 14 of the regulation reads:
Unless it is established to the satisfaction of the board that such person is not an essential worker in agriculture.
It is very difficult for the board to decide upon a thing like that. As soon as the formality is completed I do not see how the board can say, without asking for further

evidence, that a farmer is not an essential worker in agriculture. Of course the matter is most delicate, and I understand the difficulties of the minister, because there are some draftees who are under him until they go to the army, and then if while they are in the army they ask for leave, their case is decided by the board, which is under the authority of the minister. It is a most difficult situation; I understand the difficulties of the minister and I sympathize with him. Many a time I have been sent by his department to the Department of National Defence and by the Department of National Defence to his departs ment, just to know who was responsible. Of course I understand very well that the registrars, who are far from Ottawa, have not the same opportunity to telephone to both departments in order to come to some agreement about it.
If I understand the matter aright the men are under the Minister of National War Services so long as they have not gone into the army, and when they are in the army they are under the Minister of National Defence.
That is correct.

When they ask for leave
and the leave is granted by their commanding officer it is of course a shorter leave, but then I presume they are still under the Department of National Defence. What I want to know is this: When they first get into the army and when they get leave from the national war services board, during that leave are they under the Minister of National War Services or the Minister of National Defence?

If the application for
leave comes from an R recruit, that is a person who has actually reported to a training centre, the leave is not granted by a national war services board but by the national defence unit. The application has come to the board for its recommendation; the actual leave is granted by an officer of the Department of National Defence, and the person who is on leave is still subject to the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence, because he is still a soldier in the reserve army.

May I be permitted a
supplementary question? I received a letter this morning from a young man in Saskatchewan who had served one month in January, 1941. Lately he was recalled, and he applied to the board in Saskatchewan for a postponement, which was refused. Am I right in telling that young man to apply to the commanding officer of the unit to which he has now been called, or what is the situation?

War Appropriation-War Services

As soon as the thirtyday man had done his thirty days he was taken on the strength of a militia unit and thereby became a member of the reserve army, and subject to the reserve army regulations. Then each month the Minister of National Defence breaks up his requisition for men into so many new men who have done no training at all and so many who have done the thirty-day training but are to be recalled. When we recall a thirty-day man we do so for the Department of National Defence and in the name of the Minister of National Defence. It is a service we render for the Department of National Defence. We are authorized to deal with his application for postponement.

How do these young
farmers know? This is a young farmer who owns his own land in Saskatchewan; apparently he does not know where to apply for postponement.

He will get his notice;
it will be sent to him actually by our board.
He has had that.
And he may apply to our board for postponement.
He has done that.

Then if his application
for postponement has been heard by the board and has been refused-
That has been done.

-that means he automatically is recalled and must report to the training centre. He is still however a member of the reserve army, of the militia unit to which he was attached when he finished his thirty days. There is nothing to bar him from applying to the commanding officer of his unit for leave, and as I see it he is the only person to whom he may apply for leave.

What about the order
in council of March 21?

Order in council P.C. 1916, passed I think on March 12, applied only to persons who had been in the reserve army for less than three months. I do not think those regulations apply to the thirty-day men. But while they technically do not apply I believe the boards have heard applications for leave from those men. There is a difference between an application for postponement, which the board does determine, and an application for temporary leave. I hope I have made it clear to my hon. friend.
44561-159}
Not quite. If the hon. member for Temiscouata will forgive me for pursuing this point, the order in council does not apply to the thirty-day men.
I would not think so, because it applies specifically only to R recruits who have been in a training centre not more than three months.
This man has been in a training centre less than three months.
But he has belonged to a unit for more than three months.

But immediately after the thirty-day training period was over he became attached to a reserve militia unit and therefore became subject to the reserve army regulations. Perhaps I should refer to the specific order in council.

There is a great deal of confusion about this. Here is a young man who thought he came under the order in council, so he simply applied for postponement. Now he is doing his spring seeding, looking after his cattle and horses. He is alone on his farm. As a neighbour he has his father, who is a sick man. Suddenly he is called up; apparently he has applied for postponement and has been refused. He wants to know what he can do next. He is wondering how on earth he can dispose of his cattle and horses, and comply with the regulations.
He has applied for postponement, and his application has been refused by the Saskatchewan board?
Yes, although he is a genuine farmer, owning his own land.

army. Ordinarily the army looks after applications for leave. However, the reasons for embarking upon this policy are as follows. First, it was desirable to deal with these applications for leave as uniformly as possible across Canada. No matter how great an effort is made it is not possible to obtain absolute uniformity. The purpose of that proviso is curative. It is not the governing part of the regulations; it is intended to ensure that persons who ought not to be covered by the regulations will not be covered by them, and it has no other purpose. Consistently with government policy in the matter, the intent of the regulations is that all persons wholly or mainly employed in agriculture, as the term is defined in the regulations, shall be held for the purposes of agriculture, held for the particular purpose that I mentioned earlier this afternoon. It is curative so that there will be no abuse of the regulations.

Please allow me to proceed. The intent of the regulations was set out by	the Prime Minister	in	the speechthat he	made	in this house	on	March 24,and the intent is also contained in the regulations. I think I have indicated the intent in the remarks I have just made. This means, as I think I clearly stated in the press release, that there has been a fundamental change of approach with regard to persons	wholly	or mainly employed in agriculture,	within	the meaning	of	that term.
Previously the regulations were based upon the idea that the man who was physically fit might be postponed as to his military training on one ground or another, but that when that period of postponement was concluded he was meant for the armed forces of this country. These new regulations make a change in that approach; for they provide that when this man gets his postponement order, until further notice he is allocated to the purposes of agriculture. That is the intent of the regulations. There has been a shift of base with regard to the regulations. That is now the governing policy.
Individual cases will come up. A man who is wholly or mainly employed in agriculture must make his application for postponement if he desires postponement; when

In most of the cases that come up, I would say in the vast majority of cases, there are no difficulties at all. But there may be individual cases. Let us take some individual cases, the kind or type of case that might come up, just as an illustration.
Suppose there is a family of five sons, and one of the sons is called up. The board must grant that man's application for postponement unless it is established to the satisfaction of the board that he is not an essential worker in agriculture. The onus is a negative onus, which is very often a difficult onus to discharge. Essential to agriculture does not necessarily mean essential to a particular farm. "Not essential to agriculture" is a question of fact, to be found by the board in the light of all the circumstances. I do not think I could go further than that, after indicating what the policy is and also indicating, as I wish to do specifically, that the proviso is purely curative, purely for the purpose of preventing possible abuses of the regulations. The proviso is not the governing part of the section. All the questions under that are questions of fact, to be found by the board in the light of all the circumstances concerning that particular person's case. In view of the attitude taken by the minister that he would welcome any suggestions that might be offered to improve the operation of the regulations under which men are called for service and under the provisions of which postponements are granted, I have a few suggestions to offer. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) spoke in the house on March 24 he left the people of Canada under the impression that in so far as farmers were concerned, they would be entitled generally to postponement. This same idea was conveyed in the April, 1942, issue of "Canada at War", where it is stated at page 8:
Emphasizing the vital role being played in this war by food, farmers, their sons and farm labourers are granted an indefinite postponement of compulsory military service if they are doing essential farm work.
Without entering in any way into a discussion as to whether or not the announcement made by the Prime Minister was generally acceptable to those engaged in agriculture, I do say that such principle was enunciated by him and restated in "Canada at War". What is being contended this afternoon, and as I contended on April 23, is that the major complaint is to the "un-uniformity", if I may use that expression, of the administration of the regulations, and it is to this that criticism is being particularly directed. The regulations are all right, but there is nothing in them whereby any board can be required to live within their terms. There is only one way in which an individual may insist under our law on the performance of a duty by an administrative body, and that is by way of mandamus or by way of one of the prerogative writs. AH those rights have been taken away by the regulations. Therefore, when it is said that the regulations are mandatory, that means nothing. It just means that something shall be done, but if it is not done there is no right on the part of him against whom there has been discrimination to enforce his legal

rights. In other words, if a person had all the rights in the world and was not in a position to enforce those rights, they are non-existent unless the administrative body charged with the administration of the law is prepared to follow the law.

Just before six o'clock I was dealing with the regulations which establish the rights of persons who are called up for service to seek postponement. I think we shall all agree that when postponements are to be granted they should be granted in an equitable manner to the end that in the interpretation and administration of the regulations there shall be as nearly as possible uniformity in all the provinces. As the regulations stand to-day, the only appeal that can be taken is an appeal to the board in each of the provinces, the decision of the board being final. The result of that may very well be that in one province the board will interpret the regulations in a manner different from the interpretation given in another province. As the regulations are, while in one province a man may be granted a postponement when he applies, on the basis of being a person "wholly or mainly employed in agriculture", in another province the board may not see fit, on similar facts and under similar circumstances, to grant such postponement.
It was stated by the minister that the wording is mandatory, that is to say, that the board "shall from time to time, upon the application of a person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture", grant him a postponement. True enough, the section is mandatory; but there is no provision whereby a person entitled to his postponement and denied that postponement may make further application either by way of appeal or to the courts. Under the regulations, section 8 provides:
No proceeding authorized or pending before an appeal board, and no decision of a board, shall by means of an injunction, prohibition, mandamus, certiorari, habeas corpus or other process, issuing out of court, be enjoined, restrained, stayed, removed or subjected to review or consideration on any ground whether arising out of alleged absence of jurisdiction in an appeal board, nullity, defect or irregularity of the proceedings, or any cause whatsoever, nor shall any such proceedings or decision be questioned, reviewed or reconsidered.

War Appropriation-War Services
A reading of that section establishes clearly that regardless of the merits an individual may have to obtain a postponement, he is denied that right, and the prerogative writs that ordinarily prevail under British law to assure to a person, who is entitled to the mandatory performance of an act, have been denied under that section. The result is that in parts of the country, a strict and stringent administration is taking place, while in other provinces, upon similar facts, postponements are being granted.
I think the minister will agree that if one thing must be insisted on, it is that in the administration of these regulations there should be, as nearly as humanly possible, uniformity; otherwise the result may well be that a feeling of suspicion may be aroused. In my opinion the minister should donsider the setting up of a final appeal board similar to that provided by the Military Service Act in 1917, whereby, by appointment of the governor in council, one of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada should act as a central appeal judge. In that way, if any provincial board is failing to carry out properly the provisions of the regulations, or in so doing is discriminating against any person within its jurisdiction, there may be an appeal to the central authority. Only in that way can we secure uniformity of administration consistent with the proper application of the law.
While in the matter of appeal it might be argued that if it was not necessary for men called up for service to have to report until such time as the decision was handed down, the difficulty that might arise on appeals being taken could very well be obviated by a provision denying a stay of proceedings pending the decision. This afternoon someone suggested that if a man was called up and was entitled under the regulations to postponement, but had been refused and failed to report and was prosecuted, he would then have the opportunity of stating to the court that he had been Wrongly called, being entitled to his postponement and could successfully defend himself. But a reading of section 30 shows otherwise:
Every man called out pursuant to these regulations who fails or refuses to submit himself for medical examination within the time limited by and in accordance with the terms of any notice given to him by the divisional registrar requiring him to submit himself for medical examination shall be guilty of an offence.
Section 31 provides:
Every man called out pursuant to these regulations and placed by an examining physician in a category in which men so placed are considered fit for military training who fails or refuses to report within the time limited . . . shall be guilty of an offence.
Therefore the position of affairs is this. Regardless of the merits of his case a man has no right to-day to ask the crown or the military authorities to show cause on an appeal to a central appeal court or by resort to a prerogative writ that he is not entitled to postponement. It would have been much better, instead of having the National Resources Mobilization Act administered under regulations, to have made provision by statute as was done in the Military Service Act of 1917. The regulations as they are to-day are so worded that they deny to many the right to postponement, who are entitled to that postponement and, on the other hand, might operate against the crown where postponement might be granted arbitrarily by the provincial board, whereas under the facts of the case postponement ought not to be granted.
I suggest that the minister give consideration to the establishment of a judicial final tribunal here in the city of Ottawa. It is not going to be a costly proceeding. It will do no harm, nor will it delay the military effort of this'dominion, but it will assure one thing and that is that the man who lives, say in Prince Edward Island and is called up to service will know that the same type of administration is going to be applied in his case as is being followed in British Columbia. To have any other basis of administration may raise suspicion as between province and province, denied as a man is to-day those rights of British jurisprudence which assure him the performance of mandatory rights under the law. To-day a man who is called up for service has certain mandatory rights under the regulations, but if they are denied to him he has no recourse at law. He cannot go to the minister and say, "There has been a decision made against me and I am entitled to a postponement". The door is closed to the most definite rights provided for by regulation.
If the idea that I suggest is accepted, the minister will be relieved of the many hundreds of applications that are to-day being made to him. If I understood him aright this afternoon, representations are made to him regularly, and upon receiving them he communicates with the provincial boards. In that case, where one man in consequence of representations made by the minister secures postponement, while another man under similar circumstances who does not make application is ordered up for service, there is bound to be suspicion which might very well be obviated by the simple expedient of appointing as a judicial final tribunal composed of a judge of the Supreme Court of Canada.
I would suggest, too, from a reading of these regulations that they contain many incongruous provisions, and they might very well be

submitted, if not to parliament itself, with a statute introduced in that behalf, at least to a committee of parliament to the end that equality will be secured among all the people across this dominion and that uniformity of administration will be ensured.

I should like at the outset to express my great appreciation of the contribution to the discussion made by the hon. member for Lake Centre. He has put forward in a clear-cut manner the argument that there ought to be established a central court of appeal or board of appeal which would hear appeals from all the divisional boards across Canada with a view to obtaining uniformity of decision. I appreciate very much indeed the argument that he has put forward and the clarity of his statement of the grounds for it.
The general opinion thus far has been against the setting up of a central court of appeal, and in coming to that view the authorities had in mind the experience of the last war-the Military Service Act, with its great multiplicity of tribunals, and its appeals ending with an appeal to the Chief Justice of Canada. Some of those appeals dragged on for months. It was with the deliberate purpose of avoiding a repetition of what occurred then that the divisional boards were set up, each one presided over by a superior court judge or a judge of some other court in the province where the major portion of the administrative division was located.
I imagine it was for that reason also that provisions were put into the statute to the effect that the decisions of the administrative boards should be final, that they should not be reviewable by mandamus or injunction or the other various procedures to which the hon. member for Lake Centre referred. He has quoted two sections of the regulations, sections 8 and 30 which, I think, make that intent clear.
The expectation was that the questions involved in an application for postponement are questions of fact. I do not think any questions of law are involved. Perhaps when I make that statement I make it a little too broad. Let me content myself by saying that in the main all the questions that come before these boards are questions of fact. Questions of fact are not all the same. The considerations operating in each one of the provinces are not all the same. But if you ask a board presided over by a superior court judge to deal with questions of fact that come before the board you go a long way toward uniformity, perhaps as far toward uniformity as it is possible to go when you are dealing with questions of fact.

It is quite true that when you have questions of fact coming before boards, one board may attach greater weight to one particular fact than another board might do. Then, too, considerations in the various provinces differ. One province may be mainly agricultural, with the board thoroughly understanding the importance of agriculture. In another province the main activity may be industrial, with the board in that particular case having a thorough appreciation of, let us say, the needs of war industry. All of these considerations may affect the board in its dealing with the facts of each case as it comes before it.
We have had two conferences with the chairmen of the boards and the registrars. There was a conference fairly early in the history of the regulations, and then on April 23, 24 and 25 we had a three-day conference with a view to having a general discussion of the regulations and their administration. Conferences of that sort will, I think, go a very considerable way toward bringing about uniformity. I doubt whether uniformity could be any more effectively brought about by a court of appeal. If questions of law were involved, certainly it would be desirable to have a central court of appeal. But when each case is really dependent on questions of fact I do not see how the establishment of a central court of appeal could bring about uniformity. That is my view. But I appreciate very keenly the necessity of uniformity of administration of the regulations across Canada as far as that is possible in the light of the fact that the decisions in these cases are made by tribunals which are judicial tribunals, on the basis of the facts of each individual case.
We held this conference of chairmen and registrars of divisions. We sat for three days. I was present at all the sessions, and I can assure hon. members that a great deal of useful work was done. It was the view of that conference, indeed, it was the view of the department, that the regulations should be gone over from beginning to end, and it was suggested that a committee should be struck for the purpose of going over the regulations. A number of regulations that are still in the brochure of regulations as printed are spent, by reason of the facts that they were meant to cover being no longer applicable. For example, certain regulations in regard to students were applicable only to the state of affairs that existed when we called men for only thirty days. Some of these regulations should be struck out. Then it was the general view that the Minister of National War Services might appoint a committee for the purpose of going through the regulations from start to

When I was before the house last Monday I was in course of making a statement, but I did not get anywhere near through. Perhaps it is just as well. On application.

being made; and the onus rests to the crown to establish that the individual does not come within the purview of the general postponement provision.

Yes, and that

could be allowed to a central court only after that court had been applied to and had granted the right of appeal? I do not believe there should be an automatic appeal, but I think there should be provision for appeal, to the end that those entitled to rights under the law may obtain those rights. To-day, as matters now stand, the people of Canada may find themselves in the position that in one province men will be granted postponements while in another province under similar circumstances men will be called to service. It was never intended that regulations should be interpreted in a manner that would discriminate in favour of one province as against another. An appeal body would bring about uniformity in the interpretation of the regulations. This afternoon the minister stated that the regulations were mandatory; that the applicant had his rights; that they were not declaratory rights but were rights assured to him. So I put this proposition to the minister. If in any province, as a result of the predilictions or the attitude of a board, the provisions of the regulations are deliberately flouted and disregarded, what rights has an individual so affected? As I see it, he has none. He has been denied the prerogative rights such as writs of habeas corpus and certiorari. He has been denied any appeal. He has rights, but he has no method of enforcing them.
Then take the other position, in which the board would grant postponements without regard to the regulations, deliberately flout the regulations in the other direction, allowing everyone postponement without regard to whether or not, under the law, they are entitled to it. Is there any provision whereby the crown may prevent that abuse of power? There is nothing whatever under the regulations as they stand to-day; and with all the sincerity that I can put in my words I say to the minister that the enforcement of these provisions must be done equitably and fairly. To-day we find ourselves in this position, that in one province 2-3 per cent of the young men are being called up, while in another province, in proportion to population, 5-7 per cent are being called up. Continue this course and the result will be not chaos but the destruction of national unity. As I see it, there is only one way of preventing such a condition of affairs, and that is through a uniform application of the law to every person in Canada, without regard to provinces or the boards having jurisdiction in the several provinces. As the regulations are, in Saskatchewan-and I speak of that province because I represent a constituency there-every man engaged in agriculture might be called up and ordered to report, even with 
the regulation as it is, and there is no power whatsoever to interfere with the actions of the board. That would amount to a denial of justice, a denial of fairness, a discrimination against those entitled to postponement, and there is no right on the part of those who are discriminated against to appeal to the courts of this country.
It is true that in 1917 the prerogative rights were denied. I can understand the reason for that, because if it were left open to those called for service to take advantage of legal technicalities, they would do so; they would appeal by way of certiorari, habeas corpus or anything else available. But there remained the right of appeal. To-day there are no rights, either to the men who are being called up, to assure them of fair treatment, or to the crown, if a board should deliberately flout the regulation. While I have mentioned Saskatchewan, I think it only fair to say that in doing so I was not referring to that board. The Saskatchewan board is composed of three reputable gentlemen: the chairman of the board, Mr. Justice Embury, who was a brigadier-general in the last war, with a distinguished record; Mr. Bickerton, president of the United Farmers, and Mr. Carl Stewart, K.C., a member of the legislative assembly.
Might I ask the hon. member which board he is referring to when he uses the phrase "flouts the regulation?"
It would apply to any board.

That is the point. I mentioned Saskatchewan as an example of what might take place, because Saskatchewan is mainly agricultural. I could have mentioned any other province, but that was why I came back to point out that I was not specifically referring to the board in Saskatchewan. I do ask the minister to give consideration to this matter. As the regulations are, there is not a lawyer anywhere who could advise anyone as to his rights under these regulations. I do not understand why men called up were denied representation by counsel before the provincial boards, but that is what the regulations provide. If a man is denied legal representation, at least he should not be denied those ordinary rights that British subjects everywhere have enjoyed for the past two hundred and fifty years. I do not believe in wholesale appeals;

regulations, namely to enable the Department of National War Services to fulfil the requisitions sent to it by the Department of National Defence.

And do so as equitably as possible. As a matter of fact I think hon. members will be interested in the considerations which govern the assignment to a civilian rather than a defence department of this particular task of calling men for military training. I believe I can say that the Department of National War Services and the national war service boards regard as individuals all persons coming before them as a result of the notice relating to medical examination. Before the minister leaves the discussion of the regulations, I wish to say a few words in support of the position taken by the hon. member for Lake Centre. Last year the minister will remember I strongly opposed the removal of regulation 14, which took away from the applicant the right of appeal to the minister as a final court of appeal.
Where is that in any previous regulation?
Clause 14 was withdrawn, the clause appointing the minister as final court of appeal.
It is news to me.

It is not
news to the minister that the boards became the final court of appeal, that no appeal to the minister was allowed any more.
There was no appeal to the minister.
In the original regulations there was.
No.

I will not argue the point now. The minister has just said that these regulations are important and that they are becoming increasingly important. That is true, because these regulations are the machinery under which Canada proposes to requisition the lives of its citizens. As the minister acknowledged, it is most essential that these regulations and the administration set up under them shall be carried on in the most impartial manner possible. The protest has been made before and was made again to-day that there is lack of uniformity in the administration of the different boards. Last year some reference was made to a hockey team as an illustration. There are other illustrations, some of which I shall draw to the minister's attention in a moment. In my opinion it is bad practice to set up across the country quasi-judicial bodies and give to them arbitrary power under regulations which they themselves are the sole authority in interpreting. Under these regulations wide powers are given; there are blank spaces under them where it is not clear exactly what course is to be followed. In these cases the board becomes a law unto itself, and there is danger, especially if the minister lacks time for supervision or lacks firmness, of these semi-judicial bodies becoming little czars in their own domain.
Not being a lawyer, I am not sure that the procedure suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre, that a final court of appeal here in Ottawa would meet the situation, would be the best. It may be that it would. Certainly I think this would help to meet it, that first of all these administrative committees, national war services boards, ought to be conducted to some extent on the basis of court procedure.
A board is set up in Saskatchewan, for instance, with three men on it. A young man comes before that board making application
2528	COMMONS
War Appropriation-War Services
for postponement. The only representative that I know of who has ever gone before that board in addition to the person making the application is the representative of the Department of National Defence. I do not know of any representative of the labour supply board; I dc not know of any representative of agriculture other than one of the members of the board. The young man is in a court in which the Department of National Defence has a person functioning practically as prosecuting attorney, and is left to defend himself and present his own case. Most of us know what it means to be suddenly placed before a committee; the average person, if he has no experience in presenting facts, if he is timid about answering questions, can trip himself up in a very few minutes. It seems to me that if the board is made the final court of appeal, there ought to be a person, say the judge, in this case the chairman, as referee; there ought to be someone in that board presenting the case for the Department of National Defence, and there ought to be someone there who will examine the facts concerning the applicant and present the facts for him.
The average young man has not a chance in the world in presenting his own case; he is entirely at the mercy of the mood, the persuasion or the mental outlook of the men on the board. If they are considerate, thoughtful; if they examine his case carefully, help him in bringing out the facts, he may get a fair deal. If they are not that kind of men, the situation is quite different.
The set-up of these boards might well be changed. There ought to be, but as far as I know in Saskatchewan there is not, a representative of labour selected and recommended by labour; there ought to be a representative of agriculture, suggested by agriculture. In the case of Saskatchewan there is one who, I am sure, is quite satisfactory to agriculture in that province; I do not know anyone who would fill the position better. But someone on that board ought to appear on behalf of the applicant, someone who will examine his case and present it. The representative of the Department of National Defence is there, who is very naturally prepared to present many reasons why the postponement should not be granted; it is his job to get as many persons into the army as possible. Certainly someone ought to be there to present the other side of the story. If these boards are to continue to have the tremendous powers that have been given them, there ought to be some setup to make them more judicial in character and to guarantee to the persons going before them the best possible presentation of their case.

The minister says that one of the reasons why it would be impossible +o set up a final court of appeal is that these are cases founded on fact, not on interpretation of the law. That is correct. But I would ask the minister what machinery is set up by his department for the collecting of these facts. It may be better now; I have some reason to believe it is, but I know that for quite a while the facts were collected in the strangest manner. I had a young man come to my home one morning with his grandmother, whose sole support he was alleged to be. They had made an application for postponement on the ground that if this young man should be called up, the grandmother would have to leave the farm, dispose of the stock, move into town and live alone. The postponement was granted. A few days before the time to report, however, the young man was notified that the postponement had been cancelled. He came to see me; I told him there was nothing I could do, that this was the decision of the board, but that I would telephone the board and find out why the postponement had been cancelled. I called the secretary of the board, and again I have no quarrel with that gentleman. He has always been very courteous and fair to me, and he is the servant of the board, not responsible for the policy pursued. He said, "Yes, we did grant postponement, but on the basis of certain information given to us in the last few days we have cancelled that postponement." I said, "Well, that is fine, except that I should like to know the source of that information." He replied, "We are not going to tell you the name of the person." I said, "I do not want to know the name of the person, but I do want some assurance that the information reached you through proper channels. Was it secured for you by the mounted police? Was it secured for you by any officer or employee of the government?" His -reply was, "No. This information was telephoned to us by some individual in the community in whom we have confidence." Well, Mr. Chairman, if you ever start to collect your facts on that basis you are taking the most dangerous ground possible upon which to administer selective service. If the government is going to turn certain people in the community into official informers, it is storing up a lot of grief for itself. There is not a community anywhere in which there are not at least two or three people who like minding the business of other people better than their own, who specialize in sending anonymous letters, making anonymous telephone calls, or sending messages about somebody else whom for some reason or another they do not like. In all fairness I must say that in a number of cases

War Appropriation-War Services
with which I am familiar the investigation was made by the mounted police. With that I am in complete agreement; the machinery for collecting these facts ought to be official machinery. Facts ought to be collected through the proper agencies, the mounted police, the local magistrate, or some person in an official capacity who has training in sifting facts and presenting evidence.
A few moments ago I said that these boards had wide powers and that there was always the danger, in connection with semi-judicial boards of this kind, that they might become little czars in their own communities. They are pretty well the final authority; they make the decisions as to how the regulations shall be interpreted. Let me give one illustration of that; I refer to the method by which conscientious objectors have been handled, particularly in Saskatchewan. I know the subject of conscientious objectors is not a popular one; but the test of any democracy is how it treats its unpopular minorities.

Hear, hear; I entirely
agree.

I want to direct the attention of the minister to the regulation which, as he knows, is No. 19. It states:
Any man who claims that he conscientiously objects to bearing arms or to undertaking combatant service may, at his own expense, apply for an order or direction of the board postponing his military training which order or direction may be given by the board to the divisional registrar if the board is satisfied that such man conscientiously objects to bearing arms or to undertaking combatant service.
I direct the attention of the committee to the words, "if the board is satisfied," which is a wide discretion. Then regulation 20 provides:
Notwithstanding anything contained in the next two preceding sections, the board, of its own motion or on application made by the minister or any person representing the minister, in the case of any person entitled to postponement of military training, either as a Mennonite or as a Doukhobor or as having been found by the board to object conscientiously to bearing arms or undertaking combatant service, may direct that such person, if medically fit for military training, be required to report as or after his age class has been called out to carry out such alternative training, service or work as the board may direct. . . .
From what information I can gather-and of course the minister will correct me if I am wrong, because he is in a position to know all the facts in reference to every province, while I can speak only with reference to my own province-the treatment of this particular group has not been uniform in the various provinces. As an example I mention two young men whom I have known for fifteen
or twenty years. They are twins, students at the theological seminary of the United Church, studying for the United Church ministry in . Saskatoon. Both made application to the board in Regina, claiming that they had religious scruples against the bearing of arms and offering to do any type of alternative service the board might prescribe. One young man was granted postponement on the ground that they considered him to be a sincere-and I underline the word "sincere"-conscientious objector. The other young man, for some reason I have never been able to find out, was not considered by the board to be a sincere conscientious objector and, with a number of others, had his postponement refused.
They went back to the university and made an offer to the board that they were prepared to do anything else. At the university other students who normally would be called out with their age groups are given an opportunity to take the R.O.T.C. course during their spare time in order to not break into the university year. These young men asked that they be given some alternative training during their spare time, instead of the R.O.T.C. course. That was refused in Saskatchewan, though my understanding is that at the university of Toronto such training is provided for students who conscientiously object to the bearing of arms. There I believe they are given an opportunity to take alternative training in some other line. But these young men were refused that opportunity, though it is expressly provided in regulation 20 that the board may prescribe some alternative training or service.
If they are found to be conscientious objectors.

Yes, but they must have found them to be conscientious objectors, because they did not insist on calling them up for military training. They said, "All right. You will not take the R.O.T.C. course; you do not want to report for military training, therefore you must stop your university year right now and go up to Banff national park," to work in a labour gang building highways, at 50 cents a day, out of which they must buy their clothing and all the other things they require. I know of one young man who was within a few months of finishing a chemistiy course, which would have enabled him to do great service to this country in our war effort. Several of these young men have been taken out of the university in the middle of their year, and sent up to Banff national park. As I said before, and wish to make perfectly clear, I have no objection at all to these young men doing alternative service. My contention is that any man who lives in this country is in the position



War Appropriation-War Services
where the state has the right to demand from him in this emergency some form or another of service.
Practical service.

Yes, practical service.
To go back to the young man to whom I referred, he went to the board and said, "I am quite prepared to go to England with a firefighting group. I am prepared to go to England or anywhere else to drive an ambulance." But they replied that they had no arrangements for that sort of thing, and that they could not do that. The result is that we send a man to a labour gang, building roads, when it seems to me there are far more useful things we could do with young men of that kind.
I wish to repeat that I do not propose to be placed in a false light when I present this case to the minister. I have never held, and do not now hold, the view of the conscientious objector. I myself took the reserve officers training course when I was at university. In talking to these young men I have told them that in my opinion they should take the course, and that they could do so without violating their principles. I have told them that the course would do them a world of good. But I do insist that whatever one may think of the point of view of the conscientious objector, no man or group of men should be allowed to vent any sadistic tendencies they may have against any person with whose particular point of view they happen to be in disagreement.
Simply to take a young man out of a university, when hundreds of others are being left in the universities, and send him to a labour camp where he is not needed, because he antagonizes those who do not agree with his point of view, is not fair. It seems to me we are on very dangerous ground when we do that sort of thing.
Questions with respect to conscientious objectors-and I use that purely as an illustration-along with many other parts of these regulations ought to be clarified so that there will be uniform application in the administration of the regulations. There ought to be a final court of appeal, or there ought to be provision for farmer and labour advocates on the boards to present the cases of these young men in a proper and judicial manner.
Just one other point. The other evening I drew the attention of the minister to the young men who reported for training on April 9, and I pointed out then that there was a great deal of confusion in view of the fact that on March 25 the newspapers of Canada

carried a statement that they were exempted- that was the term used-and that postponement had been granted. The term used was that they were exempted from military training. I hold in my hand a clipping from the front page of a western newspaper. It is headed, "Main points of new programme" and is dated at Ottawa, March 24. It opens with these words:
Following are the high-lights of the national selective service programme, as announced in the House of Commons to-day by Prime Minister Mackenzie King.
Then follows a long list of the key-notes in the announcement, and No. 8 in the list is as follows:
Exemption from compulsory military training for essential farm workers, and prohibition against farm workers quitting jobs for nonessential work.
That is just a misunderstanding.

Yes, but it was a misunderstanding that had disastrous effects. As I said the other day, if one young man read that and did not report, he could still make application under the new order in council P.C. 2252. If he could substantiate the fact that he was working on the farm, or had been a farmer on March 23, he could get his postponement. But the other young man, who had not time to make the application, was in a different position.
