It is a subject with which it is not easy to deal, because the number of classes and kinds of persons is so varied. We cannot speak of conscientious objectors as being one class of person. In the main, conscientious objection is an individual objection toward taking human life. It varies with people. Certain persons have no objection to using force, depending upon the person against whom they may have to use the force. Some Jehovah's Witnesses believe in the use of force if it is for the purpose of defending another Jehovah's Witness, but otherwise they may be against the use of force. There are varieties of views, but generally speaking we deal with the subject of conscientious objectors under three sections of the regulations. I dealt with this at some _length last November, but I shall review the situation briefly as it is and then deal with the steps that we have taken with regard to conscientious objectors. Section 18 (1), which deals with Mennonites and Doukhobors, reads:

Members of the denomination of Christians called Mennonites and members of the community of Doukhobors who immigrated to Canada pursuant to the arrangements evidenced by the order in council of August 13, 1873, and by the order in council of December 6, 1898, respectively, or the descendants of such immigrants who have continued without interruption to be members of the aforesaid sect or denomination of Christians or of the aforesaid community of Doukhobors and who have resided without interruption in Canada, shall be entitled, subject as provided in these regulations, to the postponement of their military training.
That section deals with two classes of persons, Mennonites who come under the order in council of August 13, 1873, and Doukhobors who come under the provisions of the order in council of December 6, 1898. Persons who come within the provisions of section 18 are entitled to postponement of their military training. Applicants who come within the terms of this regulation must apply and must show, first, that they are descendants of these immigrants; second, that they have continued without interruption to be members either of the aforesaid sect or denomination of Christians, that is Mennonites, or of the aforesaid community of Doukhobors, and, third, that they have resided without interruption in Canada.

I gladly gave way a few minutes ago so that the hon. member for Kootenay West might ask a question. Half an hour has now expired. When the National Resources Mobilization Act came in, I opposed the last clause, namely that the government should have power to make rules and regulations. I opposed that because, with the exemptions and rules, I knew what was going to happen, that the act would be simply a political football, and the results have so shown. Are we here to get a total war or not? That is the question which the people of this country want answered. A great deal of the time spent here could have been more profitably spent. There is no reason why we should have this antiquated system of rising to ask questions about one thing and another. We should have the British system under which we could ask all these questions on the orders of the day, and the minister would save his time and the time of the house.
Two years ago I brought up this matter of conscientious objectors. I was at it for three months and nothing was done because it turned out that under the rules and regulations, which have the force of statutes, it would take a long time to act. The conscientious objectors have votes, and they are a class of voters that get what they want if they go after it.
They have no votes in British Columbia.

I belong to the Church of England which in one of the thirty-nine articles says that "it shall be lawful for Christian inen at the command of the magistrate to bear arms and serve in wars." That made the mother country the great country it is to-day. Under these rules and regulations we are taking a different system, with the exemptions proposed by the government, and the department created for that purpose. How
does it come about that we have a different system? We have the enemy at the door on our eastern coast; we have lost the command of the sea at the other door; we do not know where we are to-day. As far as all this talk about exemptions and boards set up to exempt farmers and others, amending the rules and regulations, and difficulty in getting orders in council acted on, is concerned, if Hitler comes here there will be no such things as boards, judge advocates and all that to further postponements. It seems to me that this department is nothing but an omnibus department. It gets out a lot of picture and information books after the fashion of Christmas time; it is largely in fact a Santa Claus department handing out information books, picture books and other gifts here and there, with the result that the war, instead of being primary, is the last thing thought about and is secondary to a lot of rules and regulations. There is a great deal of political undercurrent in this and other debates. I have seen it ever since the war started. When a debate opens, matters are raised which are not related to the war at all, and are secondary.
I have as much respect for and have had as much to do with farmers perhaps as any man in this house. I see their difficulties, and with two wars and a depression in between, I sympathize with them as much as any man in this house. But with this world war on which may engulf all the dominions, with the enemy now at the front door of three dominions, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, and at our own door, we should not be spending our time in discussing such matters as this, and rules and orders in council to exempt farm labour. I sympathize with the minister in having taken over such a department, but he is attempting the impossible. With the rules and regulations and exemptions it is utterly impossible for him to do his duty to the army. With few exceptions the navy and the air force have no difficulty about farmers' sons; they are just running there trying to get in.

been supported and modern methods adopted, we would not have had all this trouble. We could have had a million men under the voluntary system, with the money that has been spent by this department. It is one of the most mischievous departments we have ever had in war or peace. I do not blame the present minister for that; he has not been master all the time, but it has been so from the start. It was never intended to be anything but a political department for the benefit of certain sections of the country as against others. Here we have the granting of exemptions to conscientious objectors, all kinds of farm exemptions, munitions workers, divinity students and so on; we have boards set up, and all the rest of it. Well when Hitler comes here he will end all this very quickly; and he is not far away at the present time, if we are to believe what we are told. We face the possibility of all this.
I appeal to the minister: let us put some common sense into this system and these rules and regulations. In the first place, an act like this should have been construed strictly for all the people of Canada. The conscription act of the government which was in power during the first great war was construed in a definite, clear way. This act is not. This act has rules and regulations off it, loopholes, exemptions and all the rest of it. We have boards set up headed by judges, so that one would think one was in a court of

law, and now they are advocating that applicants for exemption should have the assistance of a lawyer, and that there be a judge advocate for the board to aid him to get off service. I have just as much sympathy as any man in the house for the people of the prairie provinces, who have had to go through two wars and a depression. We have a lottery system in connection with the calling up of recruits. Surely that was never intended under the act or to have such rules and1 regulations off it. Lotteries are illegal under the criminal code; yet under some of the provisions of this act numbers are put into a hat and drawn to determine who shall be called up. Such a farce! I have spoken to a number of soldiers, and they complain that some men are allowed to come home to the farm while others are not. City men must stay. Only last Saturday one young soldier told me that one man in his unit, who had a brother and sister working in a munitions plant in the city, was going to get an exemption in order to go home and work on the farm. The Grenadiers, the Queen's Own and the other regiments crossed lake Superior in the dead of winter, with the weather 46 degrees below zero, to save the prairie country, and Canada from being dislocated, and they never had any such system as this. They were volunteers. I believe the first duty of a citizen is to defend the realm.
I do not like to bring other matters into this discussion but this is the only chance we have. I am not to blame for the system. The minister's department relates to the war, the mobilization of troops, exemptions, conscientious objectors, farm workers, and others. It also has a large publicity branch known as the information bureau which beclouds the issue. That is about the only humour I have heard since the minister took office, calling it an information bureau. This information bureau is a misinformation bureau; at least I can get no information from it and a lot of such information as is given is not correct. All it does is send out tons of literature. I think a building the size of the Toronto armouries would be required to store all the paper that is wasted by this department. The press are complaining; a great many of the editors have said they consign this literature to the waste-paper basket. This department is costing the country a huge amount of money. For
instance, at a time like this, they put out a booklet of all racial origins in Canada and dealing with farmers in the war, entitled "Canadians All" by a gentleman named Doctor Watson Kirkconnell, MA.., Ph.D. I do not know what he is doctor of, music or literature or what, but I think he is a doctor of philosophy. He is a philosopher, if you please. Well, we have had a great deal of philosophy in connection with this act, and Hitler has a philosophy of his own. This booklet-260,000 copies-has been circulated all through Canada and England, and has greatly hurt this country there. It seems that everything must have stamped on it, "Issued by authority of the Honourable J. T. Thorson, Minister of National War Services," and all that sort of thing. Separatism is rampant; one would almost think we did not belong to the British empire.
I have here another booklet, in which they quote a celebrated gentleman, Mr. L. W. Brockington, official recorder of Canada's war effort. He told the people of England and the United States, and it is on the top of another pamphlet of the department:
King George VI of England did not ask us to declare war for him; we asked King George VI of Canada to declare war for us.

While the percentage of male Canadians of all origins, twenty-one years of age and over, who served in the C.E.F., was 31-02, the figure for Canada's Jews stands distinctly higher, at 37-81 per cent.
Another misstatement of fact. I do not know whether the present minister was in the government when this book was started; I do not think he was The book was a mistake. It continues:
While, moreover, only 3-38 per cent of all Canadians in the C.E.F. received declarations for bravery and distinguished conduct, 4-52 per cent of the Canadian Jews in the C.E.F. won such declarations.
Then, he is criticizing the situation in Great Britain. Enlistments, according to the figures of 'the Minister of National Defence were [DOT]051 per cent, and those figures are not correct. So much for that book. I fail to see why the people of Canada pay for it.
Not being satisfied with that, this same gentleman appeared at a meeting of the Royal

Canadian Institute held in Convocation hall at the university of Toronto in December, 1941, and said:
. "Canada is no longer an Anglo-Saxon country in terms of national origin, and there is little likelihood that any large-scale immigration from the British isles will take place after this war is over," Professor Watson Kirkconnell told the Royal Canadian Institute in Convocation hall on Saturday night.
That statement has done untold injury in the old country. I have seen it in newspapers from the old land, and they are wondering what is the matter with Canadians, who are putting up with all these conscientious objectors, and publishing books like this in war time.
In my opinion this particular department is attempting to do the impossible. I believe in what Wordsworth said of Milton of the time of the Napoleonic wars. It is reported that Wordsworth said, "Milton, thou shouldst be living at this hour; England hath need of thee." I would substitute for that, "Gilbert and Sullivan, thou shouldst be living at this hour; Canada hath need of thee to describe what is going on in all this playing at war and with all these picture books, with the difficulty of getting men into uniform, and all that kind of thing." No wonder recruiting lagged, on again, off again, on again!
I ask: Where is the treasury board when all this is going on? We have a treasury board, and if the treasury board is not meeting I understand the minister now has power to take action and spend money anyway like water. The dead-hand of the treasury is on this department-because that is all it is, a dead-hand. They can spend money like water; they are spending all kinds of money like water; a mint of money is wasted, and yet all this kind of thing is going on in this department.
They are not satisfied with one thing. No; they have got out a proclamation in connection with the anniversary each September of the declaration of war, to come again on September 10. I do not even see the king's name in it, in connection with the proclamation. Here is a celebration of an anniversary of the war, and the king's name is not in it. More separatism. We all know that the war started the day Great Britain declared war, because when Britain is at war, so is Canada.
It started the day Canada declared war.

When Hitler and his axis ships approached the Athenia he did not say, "Oh, you have not declared war, yet." Hitler did not pay any attention to our proclamations; he just sank the Athenia, with 130 Canadians on board.

War Appropriation-War Services
I do not wish to be unfair to the minister, and I will say that I believe he is conscientious, hardworking and did not initiate this legislation. I do not know him as well as some do, but I believe he is trying to do his duty. But he is trying to do it under impossible conditions and an impossible system.
There is another gentleman in the department, the director-general, Mr. Lash, who is giving talks over the radio. One can scarcely turn on his radio without hearing this gentleman who is supposed to be the director. I asked a question on May 6 as to who authorized these Santa-Claus books, and under whose instruction this particular book was written. The answer was that it was written under the instructions of the director of public information. It is the work of the director and all his regiment of hussars. One cannot turn on the radio at night without hearing them. I shut off my radio, because I do not wish to listen to those people talk and give wrong information about Ontario recruiting. What has he been doing?- spreading seeds of disunity between Ontario and Quebec by his talks. He has given figures on active recruiting. I will say to him the figure was given last week in the above return showing that of 3S,000, there were 37,000 who applied for exemption from one province. Those are the figures, whether he likes them or not.
No wonder people are groaning under heavy taxation.	They wonder where the
trouble is, but we allow these expenditures to go on in this manner.

One point in these regulations that I cannot understand is this, that the man who is usefully engaged as a farmer may be refused an exemption, while the parasite who says he is a conscientious objector may enjoy exemption. That seems unfair. On the one hand we have a good farmer who brings his case to the board. The board says, "No; we can do nothing." And there is no power in the minister or in the government to change the decision of the board, except by abolishing that body. On the other hand there is the fellow who is always in a poolroom, and who does not work. He is a parasite, and says he is a conscientious objector. That fellow will not go to work.
It is said that in 1873, in the days of Sir John A. Macdonald and, later on, at the time of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, some concessions were made to the Doukhobors and the Men-nonites. This, again, I cannot understand. I remember on one occasion, when a former Liberal government was in office, I asked a minister why the government did not remove the exemption from tax-free bonds in 1922, as soon as they took office. He told me that they thought they had to respect a contract. Well, I find it immoral in war time to grant an exemption to Mennonites and Doukhobors, on account of some silly enactment made in the past.
It is a defiance of the people of the land to grant exemptions to these conscientious objectors. There are people who should not be given these exemptions and yet who enjoy them by virtue of the regulations and by virtue of the law. However, these regulations are no worse in that respect than was the Militia Act and the Borden conscription act of 1917. The minister will always have this matter brought up every time the farmers are dissatisfied.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) referred to the information bureau. Everyone knows my views about that. I suggested that it be reformed by abolishing it. The hon. member for Broadview gave the Toronto viewpoint, and I shall give the viewpoint of the. province of Quebec. The French director is a fascist and a neurasthenic and he is not qualified to be on the bureau. His stuff is silly; his letters are absolutely silly; it is all a waste of paper. I have complained about getting no information from this bureau. We did get some data from the Department of Munitions and Supply, but there was always something lacking. We were given the names and the amounts of money that

War Appropriation-War Services
were spent, but we were never told the quantity of goods furnished and therefore it was an impossibility to know the cost. Moreover, it was given to us in such a way that a member of parliament would need ten secretaries and ten adding machines to know how much the packers were paid in a month or something like that. It was impossible to get any real information; it was simply a list of names and the disbursements of money-the quantities were never shown. It was so bad that the mayor of Ottawa complained about it and suggested it was useless. Now that we do not have anything, we are just as well off as we were when we had those figures.
All we get from the information bureau is data about rubber and gas and oil. It is simply a detective novel published in instalments. We hear something about Mr. Cottrelle and Mr. Berkinshaw; it is simply a clearing house of matters regarding the Department of Munitions and Supply. Sometimes the literature that comes out of this office is provocative and the minister may have trouble with the people because of it. So I join with the hon. member for Broadview in asking the minister to abolish this department.
I think the minister should define the phrase "ordinarily resident". Outside of the provisions that relate to Doukhobors, Mennonites and conscientious objectors I cannot say, as does the hon. member for Broadview, that this is political legislation. I believe that under the present minister the regulations will serve the purpose for which they were drafted. What the minister needs is cooperation from the boards. He must be the guiding star of the boards. Simply because they have the right to make final decisions is no justification for their acting in contravention of the spirit of the law. The minister is the lawmaker, and when he gives an interpretation of the regulations, that interpretation should be followed.	When the boards do not do
that, the only recourse is to change them.
I do not complain about all cases, but there are some in which decisions were given without sufficient consideration to satisfy public opinion. I hope the minister will take action. He is the boss of his department and he does not need advice from any of his colleagues regarding the operation of the regulations. Members of parliament know more about the operation of the regulations in their own constituencies than do any of the ministers except the 
minister in charge of this department. When members of parliament make representations that are in the public interest I hope the minister will consider them as such. I have great admiration for him and he knows it. I want his support so that we shall have the least possible trouble in that regard.
Sometimes we have to fight to get men into the army when they want to join, but when a man is indispensable on a farm it is the duty of the board to keep him there until conditions change. This is the interpretation of the law that is expected by all. I want the minister to take what I have said in the spirit in which I have said it. My only desire is to have everything in his department run as smoothly as possible, to see that justice is given to all. When I know of some unfairness or injustice I cannot do otherwise than ask the minister to help me to redress the wrong.

I would say to the hon.
member for Temiscouata that I have noted his request for a definition of the phrase "ordinarily resident in Canada." That will cease to have anything but an academic interest in view of the announced policy of the government that the regulations will be made to apply to all residents of Canada, whether British subjects or otherwise. The Prime Minister made that announcement of policy, and it is merely a matter of working out the intricate arrangements that are involved.
The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. McDonald) raised a question with regard to the notice relating to medical examination and stated that in certain cases the person receiving the notice was not told of his right to apply for postponement. My information is that along with the notice of medical examination goes a set of instructions and that those instructions definitely indicate to the person who receives the notice what he has to do and what are his rights. In order that it may be a matter of record in the same Hansard in which is reported the remarks of the hon. member for Pontiac, I should like to put these instructions on Hansard. They are very brief. With the leave of the committee I shall do so. The instructions are as follows:
Department of National War Services Instructions
Upon receiving the enclosed "notice-medical examination" you will proceed, within three clear days, to any duly licensed doctor in your village, town or city, or at the nearest point to you. Show the doctor your "notice-medical examination" and be sure to sign the "medical examination and certificate" form used by the doctor who will examine you. You are reminded that you must proceed to the doctor at your own expense and that the department

Shipping Losses
will not pay any transportation in connection with your medical examination, but the department will pay the examining physician for examining you. Any question which you may wish to take up should be taken up in a letter addressed to your divisional registrar. His address^ appears in the upper left hand portion of the "notice-medical examination". You are also reminded that you must notify your divisional registrar immediately if you are a student at some university or college, or a member of the navy, the army or the air force, or of a non-permanent active militia unit. Should you have reason to make application for the postponement of your period of military training, do it right now to your divisional registrar. Your divisional registrar will not receive any application for postponement after eight clear days of the date appearing on the enclosed "notice-medical examination". If you are notified to report for military training you will receive a transport warrant covering only the distance from your stated place of residence to the training centre to which you will be notified to report. The department will pay no other transportation. By following the above instructions you will be serving your best interests.
Progress reported.
